newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian budget gives boost to futures trading.
newsitem.headline: Indian budget gives boost to futures trading.

text.p: India on Friday proposed to set up a global futures exchange in castor oil and allow forward trade in cotton and jute which dealers said would open the country's commodities trading to the world.
"It's a giant stride," said Bombay Oilseeds and Oils Exchange (BOOE) president Navin Shah, reacting to the proposals contained in the federal budget for 1997/98 (April/March).
The budget was presented to parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram on Friday evening.
The proposals took commodities traders by surprise as their expectations of the budget were low as it was presented by a coalition government of 15 centrist and left groups.
"We have got a very good gift. It's an opportunity to tell the world that we are moving in the right direction," said Shah.
At present, futures trading is allowed in castorseed, hessian, gur (jaggery), potatoes, turmeric and pepper.
An official committee had in 1994 recommended introduction of futures trading in cotton, oilseeds and silver. Gold and sugar could be considered at a later stage, it said.
India's first futures exchange to facilitate global trading in pepper is to become operative in April in the southern city of Kochi (formerly Cohin).
Futures trading in commodities was banned in the 1950s and 60s in a bid to stabilise prices and to end hoarding and speculation.
Trade organisations have been demanding resumption of futures trading in commodities in the last few years after India initiated an economic liberalisation programme in 1991.
Shah said the BOOE, which had been operating domestic futures trading in castorseed, could offer the necessary infrastructure for the proposed castor oil exchange.
"We will be very close to the world castor oil export market," said Shah.

India, the world's largest castor oil exporter, accounts for about 80 percent of the world export trade in the commodity. It's annual exports of castor oil average around 200,000 tonnes, valued at around 7.0 billion rupees ($195 million).
India produces about 800,000 tonnes of castorseed, 700,000 tonnes of it coming from the western state of Gujarat. The remainder comes from the southern state of Andhra Pradesh.
Shah said foreign traders and broking houses could become members of the proposed global exchange and provide much-needed know-how to their Indian counterparts.
Cotton and jute are two other commodities that Chidambaram had chosen to favour for forward trading in his budget.
"It's risk protection measure and is in the fitness of things," said East India Cotton Association (EICA) president Suresh Kotak.
"Futures and ready (delivery) are two sides of the same coin," Kotak said. "The decision to allow futures trading in cotton will greatly benefit the cotton economy."
Cotton traders have been arguing that India has now emerged as a surplus cotton producer and that restrictions on trade need to be removed.
"The proposal is in line with the government's economic liberalisation programme," Kotak said. "It will help cotton growers plan their crop well in advance."
India's cotton crop in 1996/97 (October/September) has been officially estimated at 16 million bales (one bale is 170 kgs) the same as in the previous year.
The government has so far authorised an export of 1.2 million bales in the current season against 1.59 million in 1995/96.
Kotak said EICA had the infrastructure as it had been operating futures trading in the past before it was banned.
